additions.text: To teach that respect and the other forms of regard should increase progressively among them, he states a gradation in six and a half verses beginning with “living beings.” “Nonliving” means insentient. Among these, bearers of vital breath are superior; higher still are those endowed with awareness. The activities of the senses are present even in trees in a subtle form. Thus the Mokṣa-dharma of the Mahābhārata states, “Therefore trees see; therefore trees smell,” and so forth. Of these functions, the activity of the sense of touch is the one that is manifestly evident.
Superior to those that know touch are those that know taste, such as fish; superior are those that know smell, such as bees; and superior are those that know sound, such as serpents.

Those that distinguish differences of form include crows and the like. Then come those having teeth on both sides. The sense is that many-footed creatures are superior to footless ones, quadrupeds to the many-footed, and thereafter bipeds—human beings.
Thereafter, among human beings, comes the gradation of the varṇas.

One who resolves doubt is a Mīmāṃsaka. Superior even to such a person is one who simply performs his own prescribed action. The mark of one free from attachment is that he does not milk his own dharma for personal gain; that is, he is desireless.

All actions, their objects and fruits, and even the body have been offered by him; therefore he is unobstructed and without interval. He offers them to the non-agent, being himself free from the conceit of agency.
By the enumeration of the living beings, the intended vision is that He has entered them as the indwelling controller.
He concludes the bhakti-yoga just taught together with the previously taught eight-limbed yoga, with the words “bhakti-yoga and…” O daughter of Manu, “Puruṣa” here means the Supreme Lord.

What remained of the earlier question—“describe the transmigrations of the living being and the nature of Time”—he now answers in a verse and a half. This form of Bhagavān is the controller of all. It is constituted of pradhāna and puruṣa and is also beyond and distinct from them. This itself is called daiva. From it comes the activity of karma characterized by many forms of transmigration; the transmigrations produced by actions impelled by daiva are thus diverse. This same form of Bhagavān is also called Time. It is the locus and cause of alteration, the change of things from one condition to another. Thus it was said, “From Time comes the disturbance of the guṇas,” and it will be said, “Time is the disturbance of the guṇas.” It is divine, possessed of wondrous power. By “beings,” continuing to the end of the passage, are meant the living beings who identify respectively with mahat and the other principles.

He states how Time is the cause of fear. By means of beings themselves it devours beings and destroys them. “Adhiyajña” means the giver of the fruit of sacrifice. “Of those who calculate or control” means of those who bring others under their power.
Śrīdhara Svāmī does not provide a separate explanatory block for this verse in the pinned Sanskrit file.

The terrifying nature of the Lord expressed in the śruti, “From fear of Him the wind blows,” and similar passages belongs precisely to His form as Time; this is stated in six verses beginning here. “From fear of Him” means by His impulsion. The wind blows—moving in lesser and greater measure and in different directions. The sun heats, in particular places and times, and illumines after heating; through rising and setting it shines in this ordered way.
The meaning is: because they are afraid of Him.
Because they fear Him, the rivers flow, and the earth together with its mountains shines forth and remains established.
“That sky” acts according to His regulation, that is, by His command. Mahat, the great principle, expands its own sprout-like body in the form of the worlds.
The deities who preside over and control the guṇas, Brahmā and the others, engage in the creation and other functions of this universe. “In every age” means again and again.

He is the primordial maker, producing one person, such as a son, through another, such as a father; and He is the maker of the end, causing even the destroyer, Death itself, to die through death. Yet He Himself is beginningless, endless, and imperishable.

In the thirtieth chapter the downward course, produced by tāmasic sin, of lustful persons whose minds are agitated by pampering the body, spouse, and the rest is taught. Having described the power of Time, for the sake of detachment he elaborates over three chapters the transmigration of those who perform diverse actions. “Of this powerful Time” is the construction; there is also a reading with “by the powerful one.” Though being driven and shaken by Time, a person does not know it, just as a row of clouds does not know the force of the wind.

He states that very force. Whatever object a person acquires or brings about with pain and effort, Bhagavān in the form of Time shakes and destroys that very object, for the sake of which he had labored.

He states the cause of sorrow: houses and the other possessions are connected with the body together with its dependents, such as wife and family. “Vasu” means wealth. The word “and” also gathers in other items not explicitly stated.
Showing the creature’s foolish understanding, he elaborates its suffering in fourteen verses beginning with “the creature.”
“Hellish” means a condition produced by hellish food and similar causes.
His heart has desires that have taken deep root and whose imagined projects have spread widely. “He thinks much of himself” means that he boasts, “I have accomplished my purpose.”
He is troubled by anxiety over maintenance and the bearing of his burdens.

He shows the man’s corrupt disposition. His self and senses are captivated by secret acts of sexual enjoyment arranged even by unchaste women, and by the talk of sweet-speaking children. The construction is completed by the next statement, “he considers it happiness.” Their so-called duties are full of crooked dealings concerning wealth and the like and are dominated by suffering.
He nourishes those very people by whose maintenance he sinks downward. By calling him an eater of remnants, the text indicates that even his own enjoyment is difficult and meager.
“Vārtā” means livelihood. “Without strength” means powerless. “Another’s wealth” means the property of someone else.
“Akalpa” means incapable or unable.

batches.literal_commit_message: Add literal Śrīdhara renderings for ŚB 3.30.13–3.31.8

additions.text: They no longer show him the honor that they showed before. “Kīnāśāḥ” means miserly or hard-hearted cultivators. The comparison is with an old bull that has become worn out.
“Being maintained” means being supported by others. Food is placed near him contemptuously and without respect. Like a dog that guards a house, he eats what is brought, while afflicted by disease.
His eyes protrude outward; the channels that serve as bodily passages are obstructed by phlegm; he is distressed by coughing and difficult breathing, and makes a gurgling sound.
He is surrounded and encircled by his relatives, who address him and call out, “Father!”
“Asta-dhīḥ” means one whose understanding and mental power have been lost.

For the dead there are two courses, according to merit and sin. Of these, he now describes the sinful course, beginning with the messengers of Yama and continuing to the end. He sees the two messengers whose gaze is violent and angry.
“Having covered” means having restrained, blocked, and confined him.

His heart is pierced by their threats. The construction is completed by the next verse: afflicted, he moves onward. He is overwhelmed by hunger and thirst; the road is covered with heated sand and has neither a resting place nor water.
He is brought to the abode of Yama.
He adds a particular detail: the road extends ninety-nine thousand yojanas, and, when his sin is excessive, he is carried along by the two messengers.
In four verses he briefly exhibits the torments. “Ādīpana” means being set ablaze or caused to burn. He also undergoes the eating of his own flesh, whether cut from him by himself or cut by another.
“Vaiśasa” means torment, injury, and severe affliction of one’s own person.
“Bhidāpana” means being made to split or being subjected to piercing and breaking.
Śrīdhara Svāmī does not provide a separate explanatory block for this verse in the pinned Sanskrit file.
Nor should these torments be regarded as impossible, since comparable sufferings are seen even here in this world; this is the point of the verse beginning “right here.”
“Both” means both the family and his own body.

Wealth acquired through sin may be enjoyed by many, yet the doer alone goes to hell. He leaves here the gross body that he had nourished through hostility toward living beings; what is other than merit—his sin—becomes the provision that he must experience on the journey.

An objection is raised: why should he not also leave the sin behind when he leaves the body? The reply is that, by daiva—the Lord—he is made to experience the stain and sin incurred in maintaining that family.

An objection is raised that maintenance of the family is itself prescribed. The word “merely” answers this: the “final state of darkness” is the place of hell reached by one whose activity is merely such worldly maintenance without the higher aim.

He explains the manner in which a human body is obtained again. Before the attainment of human embodiment lie all the various torments. The word “and so forth” includes births among dogs, pigs, and similar creatures. After successively undergoing all of these, with his sins exhausted by experience and having become purified, he again obtains human birth here.

In the thirty-first chapter, through a mixture of merit and sin, attainment of the human womb in this intermediate world is described as the rājasic course. The previous chapter said, “he returns here”; now that statement is shown in detail. “By karma” means by action done previously. Daiva, the Lord, is the eye and guide that leads and impels him, and thus he enters the womb.

The kalala is the mixture of semen and blood. A budbuda has a rounded form. A karkandhu is a jujube fruit; the embryo becomes hard and shaped like it. A peśī is shaped like a lump of flesh; in other kinds of womb it may instead take the form of an egg.
The formation of the limbs such as arms and feet means their differentiation and division. The sexual organ and the various bodily openings then arise.
He is covered and enclosed by the jarāyu, the membrane that surrounds the embryo.

His bodily constituents grow by means of the food eaten by the mother and by her drink and other nourishment. He lies in the disagreeable pit in which creatures arise. The Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa similarly says that a channel called Āpyāyanī is attached to the fetus at the navel and to a cavity in the woman’s intestinal region; what the woman eats and drinks passes through it, and by those substances the creature’s body is nourished and grows.
The worms present there bite and eat at him. Because of his extreme tenderness and delicacy, all his limbs become wounded.
Unbearable pains arise in all his limbs; the verb “he remains” is supplied from the following verse. Enclosed by the fetal membrane, his back and neck become bent and crooked.

additions.text: By daiva, that is, by the force of former karma, he regains memory. Remaining there for a long time in that dreadful condition, scarcely able to breathe, he remembers.
He is shaken by the bodily winds that cause delivery. “Sodara” means one born from the same womb; the comparison is with a worm born in filth within the same cavity.

“Nāthamāna” means pleading for help, or being tormented. The “seer” here is the living being who still views himself through embodiment. He is afraid of another residence in a womb. His seven bodily constituents are like bonds that confine him, and his understanding is distressed and agitated.

I take refuge in the fearless lotus feet of Bhagavān, who of His own will assumes many forms in order to protect the world. “Moving upon the earth” is said with the incarnation of Śrī Kṛṣṇa in view. It is He who has shown me, an unworthy and conditioned being, a course such as this residence in the womb, suited to what I have made for myself.

An expected question is: who is this in whom you take refuge, and what distinction exists between you and Him such that one is served and the other serves? Here, in the mother’s body, I depend upon māyā, composed of the elements, senses, and mind and transformed into bodily form; my own nature appears covered by karma and I seem bound. Yet I bow to Him who is present here as well. The word “but” indicates the distinction: though perceived in the afflicted heart, He remains changeless. He is pure, without limiting adjunct, because His awareness is indivisible and unbroken.

The source notes an alternative reading and preserves the line: “I bow to the Supreme Puruṣa of Prakṛti and Puruṣa.” The pinned source is terse and text-critical at this point, so the rendering is kept correspondingly literal.

An objection is raised: if this bondage will cease through knowledge, what is the need of bowing to the Supreme Lord? The answer is that the living being, whose memory is lost through His māyā and who wanders the road of saṃsāra under the toil produced by it, cannot regain his own true nature by any means without the grace of that great Lord. The path is marked by great actions caused by the guṇas and is deeply binding. Since knowledge does not arise without the Lord’s grace, He alone is to be served.

He establishes that the Lord alone gives knowledge. Who other than Him placed in me this knowledge whose range embraces the three times and reality itself? No one. It is the Lord alone. Could some superior living being give it? No, because all of us as living beings follow the track of karma; no one apart from Him is capable. His own capability is shown by saying that His portion follows and enters all that is stationary and moving as the indwelling controller. Therefore I worship Him.

He reports his suffering. In the cavity of another body—the hollow of the mother’s abdomen—he has fallen into a pit of blood, feces, and urine, and his body is severely heated by the digestive fire. With miserable understanding and longing to leave that cavity, he counts his months, asking, “When indeed will I be cast outside?”

Remembering the benefit that has been done for him, he speaks. “By one such as You” means by one who has no equal. May He be satisfied by His own gracious action itself; apart from the mere offering of folded hands, who could ever make a return for such a benefit?

The earlier statement that the Lord gave him “such a condition” indicated knowledge distinct from that of other species; he now explains the distinction. Another creature, such as an animal, bound by the seven bodily constituents, merely experiences bodily pleasure and pain in its embodied state. I, however, through the discriminative knowledge created and given by Him, have become possessed of a disciplined body—“dama” standing also for śama and the other disciplines. I behold the ancient, complete Puruṣa both outside and within the heart, immediately present like the indwelling consciousness, though He may appear as if the locus of ego and the enjoyer.

Repeating the distress of saṃsāra made manifest by discriminative knowledge, he resolves upon the path of liberation in two verses beginning with “that I.” O all-pervading Lord, though dwelling in the womb amid great suffering, I do not wish to go outside. The reason is that outside is like a blind well, where Your māyā approaches and envelops the creature; following that māyā there arise the false cognition “I am this body” and the wheel of transmigration through relations with spouse, children, and the rest.

Therefore, even while remaining here, free from agitation, I shall raise myself from the darkness of saṃsāra by means of my friend, the self in the form of the charioteer-like intelligence. Thus this misery of entering many different wombs through many openings will not again be mine. What means do I possess for that? The feet of Viṣṇu have been brought and established within my heart.
“Ten months” marks the moment immediately before birth. The “seer” is the living being. At that very moment he is turned downward, and the wind that causes delivery drives and pushes him forth.
He is released and cast downward.
“Rorūyati” means that he cries again and again.

Those caring for the infant do not know the intention of another. When he cries for milk, they may imagine abdominal pain and give a bitter neem preparation; when he cries from abdominal pain, they may instead give the breast, and so forth.
Being unable even to make the movements required for sitting up and rising, he continues to cry; the verb is carried over from the preceding context.
“Āma” means one whose skin is tender and delicate. The knowledge that had arisen in the womb has now disappeared.

Infancy lasts five years; thereafter comes childhood before youth, with the sufferings of study and the like. The suffering of youth is then described in three and a half verses. Because the desired object is not obtained, he is pervaded by grief, and his anger is kindled by ignorance. As the body grows, the ego and anger grow along with it, and he enters into conflicts that lead toward his own destruction.
He elaborates ignorance. With respect to the body made from the elements, false grasping produces the cognition “I” and “mine.”
He acts for the sake of that body. By the very karma through which he is bound, a body follows him, returning again and again. It is called one who is bound by ignorance and action.

If, being established among the wicked, he delights in their path—or if, even while established on a good path, he delights in association with the wicked—then he enters the darkness of hell in the manner already described, beginning with the body of torment that envelops him.

At the word “compassion,” some recensions read “austerity”; the pinned source records this as a textual note. “Those whose self is broken” means those whose understanding identifies the self with the body. Such persons become subject to women like play-animals under another’s control.

The bondage arising from association with those attached to women is such that it does not arise from ordinary association with others; hence the warning concerns association even with their associates. Just as iron permeated by fire burns, the association transmits the force of what it has entered; this is the intended comparison with other ordinary persons.

In seven verses beginning with Prajāpati he elaborates how association with women becomes a cause of misfortune. Prajāpati, taking the form of a stag, pursued one who had become a doe, having cast aside shame.

Marīci and the others were created by Brahmā; Kaśyapa and the others were created by them; and gods, human beings, and the rest were created by those descendants. Among all of them, what man indeed possesses an intellect entirely unbroken and a mind wholly unattracted?
The attraction can overcome even heroic men who have conquered the directions.
